title: Mandatory Testosterone Tests Are a Terrible Idea. A Doctor Explains Why.
text:
Mandatory Testosterone Tests Are a Terrible Idea. A Doctor Explains Why.
A veteran debunker of medical quackery examines Pete Hegseth's testosterone obsession. He finds a dangerously crude ideology of manhood dressed up as military readiness.
A guest essay by Edzard Ernst
When is a man a man? The question once preoccupied German rock star Herbert Grönemeyer in his 1984 hit “Männer” (”Men”) – and to this day, we struggle to answer it conclusively and universally. A glance inside the underwear, of course, reveals the biological reality in most cases.
But whether someone feels like a man, behaves in stereotypically masculine ways, or otherwise conforms to male role expectations is by no means settled by the presence of the equipment. In short: More than 40 years after Grönemeyer’s hit, a numerical measurement of manhood remains all but impossible.
The U.S. “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth apparently refuses to accept this. Under his plans, service members aged 30 and older will be required to undergo annual testosterone tests. Behind the initiative lies a conception of masculinity and men’s health that, on closer inspection, is highly questionable.
In a video posted to the platform X under the title “The High-T Department of War,” he holds forth on the individual war fighter as America’s “most decisive tactical advantage.” The tests, he says, are meant to ensure that soldiers have “the right testosterone levels” to perform at their best. He has repeatedly invoked the warrior ethos in the military and the ideal of the traditionally masculine fighter in the past.
Experts and medical professional societies, by contrast, recommend testosterone testing – for good reason – only for men with specific symptoms, clear risk factors, or certain preexisting conditions. Testosterone levels in healthy men can fluctuate naturally. Screening hundreds of thousands of soldiers would be a textbook case of overdiagnosis and would very likely lead to false-positive results and overtreatment as well.
The consequences of Hegseth’s bizarre idea should not be taken lightly. Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can cause considerable side effects, especially when it is not medically necessary in the first place. One possible complication is erythrocytosis, an increase in red blood cells that can promote thrombosis, strokes, or heart attacks.
The physician Edzard Ernst, born in 1948, took his first job in 1978 at a naturopathic clinic in Munich. He was a professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation in Hanover and Vienna before being appointed to Exeter, England, where he built up the world’s first chair in complementary medicine starting in 1993. He was granted emeritus status in 2012 following a conflict with the heir to the British throne at the time, Prince Charles. Ernst is considered one of the leading critical researchers of alternative medicine. He has published more than 50 books and writes regularly for various English, French, and German media outlets.
TRT can also fuel the growth of prostate cancer and impair fertility. What you will search for in vain, on the other hand, is robust evidence that TRT improves cognitive performance or physical resilience in healthy men.
